newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Security Council ends Belgrade sanctions.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Security Council ends Belgrade sanctions.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council on Tuesday formally ended the trade sanctions against the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro imposed in 1992 for their role in fomenting the war in Bosnia.
Sanctions against Yugoslavia as well as Bosnian Serbs were suspended by the council last November as a followup to their participation in the U.S.-initiated Dayton peace accords.
The council at that time stipulated that the sanctions -- a stringent trade embargo and a travel and transport ban -- would be lifted entirely after this year's Bosnian elections, held on Sept. 14.
The resolution, approved by a 15-0 vote, "terminates with immediate effect" the May 1992 sanctions.

The document warned, however, that the council would consider reimposing any of the sanctions if Yugoslavia or the Serbs failed "significantly to meet (their) obligations under the (Dayton) peace agreement." But most diplomats considered it unlikely Russia would vote to restore any of the embargoes.

To the disappointment of Russia, the resolution, at the insistence of the United States, did not end the suspension of Yugoslavia from the U.N. General Assembly and other U.N. bodies, mainly because of its disputed legal status.
It also made no provisions for Yugoslavia to rejoin financial institutions such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund.

U.S. Ambassador Madeleine Albright said Washington supported the progress made to date but more needed to be done under the Dayton peace accords. In the meantime, she said in a statement, other sanctions will stay in place

"Serbia-Montenegro will not be able to participate in international institutions, including the United Nations and the World Bank, until it makes susbstantial progress in Kosovo, cooperates fully with the International (war crimes) Tribunal in the Hague and Belgrade settles successor state issues with its neighbours," she said.

British Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind said last week that Western European states had linked Yugoslavia's re-entry into financial institutions to progress on the restive Serbian province of Kosovo, dominated by ethnic Albanians. Diplomats, however, said Britain supported Belgrade's readmission to the U.N. General Assembly.

Tuesday's resolution also did not release Belgrade's frozen assets because of disputes and claims from successor states, such as Croatia, Bosnia, Slovenia and Macedonia, after the breakup of the former Yugoslavia.

Russia's U.N. ambassador, Sergei Lavrov, said he had wanted the resolution to cover Belgrade's re-admission to U.N. bodies "but others put more linkages" into the issue than the General Assembly itself had done.
"Their only condition was that the war should stop, and the war has stopped long ago," he told reporters.
But he said lifting the sanctions should help Belgrade conduct its trade "on a firmer basis and stimulate exchanges."

Yugoslavia's U.N. envoy, Vladislav Jovanovic, told reporters the resolution was "positive both for us and the international community, which by this act fulfilled its own commitment with the Dayton peace process."
Washington this week agreed to the lift sanctions after the Sept. 14 Bosnian elections were certified on Sunday by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
